pages.text: Office buildings emptied out but are filling up again - as homes Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Office buildings emptied out but are filling up again - as homes 6 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Business reporter, Paris Evidence Paris Le Diamant office building is to close and be converted into apartments When Roland Cubin walks you round what will eventually be a new Parisian apartment you have to use your imagination. "Here you will be in the kitchen, and here is the bathroom," says the deputy CEO of French real estate company Groupama Immobilier. It all sounds appealing, an upmarket flat in the west of Paris, but presently the space doesn't look like one at all. That's because it's currently a corner of one floor of a nine-storey office building called Le Diamant, where 1,800 people work. Groupama Immobilier intends to convert the entire building into apartments. It should be the first of many such office-to-apartments conversions in the surrounding area. We are in La Défense, the purpose-built, business district of the French capital, where the city has congregated its modern skyscrapers. Mirroring a similar trend in places such as New York, Washington DC and London; Paris La Défense, the public development authority that runs the area, has unveiled plans to turn up to a fifth of the office buildings into housing. pages.text: Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Executive Order 14173: Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity Read the Executive Order On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order (E.O.) 14173, "Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity," which revoked E.O. 11246. E.O. 14173 ordered that the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP) immediately cease holding federal contractors responsible for taking affirmative action or allowing workforce balancing on certain bases. Federal contractors were in turn told to wind down compliance with E.O. 11246's regulatory scheme by April 21, 2025. In response to E.O. 14173, on January 24, 2025, then-Acting Secretary Vincent Micone issued Secretary's Order 03-2025, which ordered that OFCCP cease and desist all investigative and enforcement activity under E.O. 11246. Order 03-2025 also placed OFCCP's activity related to Section 503 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. 793 (Section 503), and the Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act, 38 U.S.C. 4212 (VEVRAA), in abeyance pending further guidance. Office of Geothermal Announces Geologic Enhanced Mapping System (GEMS) Prize The $300,000 prize will help locate hidden geothermal systems. Geothermal Technologies Office September 10, 2026 Estimated Read Time min The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Geothermal has announced the $300,000 Geologic Enhanced Mapping System (GEMS) Prize to help identify hidden geothermal systems by using geophysical data to identify faults and structures indicative of geothermal resources. The GEMS Prize challenges competitors to develop, train, and test algorithms that generate enhanced geologic fault datasets—which, in turn, can support mapping and modeling for geothermal and critical mineral resources. By using real-world datasets and testing ideas against geophysical data, the GEMS Prize is expected to accelerate discoveries of new, commercially viable hidden geothermal systems while reducing exploration and development risks. The competition comprises two rounds, with prizes ranging from $15,000 to $100,000. Both individual and group competitors can participate, and submissions are due December 3, 2026. Office of Nuclear Energy Celebrates Fifth Advanced Reactor Criticality Oklo’s Groves Isotope Test Reactor successfully achieved criticality, becoming the fifth DOE-authorized reactor to go critical this summer. Office of Nuclear Energy August 6, 2026 Estimated Read Time min WASHINGTON — Last night, as part of the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Reactor Pilot Program, Oklo’s Groves Isotope Test Reactor successfully achieved criticality. The experiment took place at the company’s facility in Lockhart, Texas. Groves is the fifth DOE-authorized advanced reactor to achieve criticality this summer, further solidifying America’s nuclear comeback. "Thanks to President Trump's precedent-setting directive to create the Reactor Pilot Program, Oklo's Groves Isotope Test Reactor is part of the revival of America's nuclear energy industry. We applaud the work of the Oklo, DOE, and Idaho National Laboratory staff who helped achieve this milestone," said Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Ted Garrish . In this regard, research software/code is identified as a research object and outcome that can also help make data more interoperable and reusable. OPP also recognizes the effort that goes into data and sample management and therefore, beyond encouraging data and sample reuse , OPP expects appropriate authorship, attribution, and citation of data, samples, and code. Office of Radiological Security (ORS) The Office of Radiological Security (ORS) makes the United States safer, stronger, and more prosperous by eliminating the risk of a radiological dispersal device, or any other malicious use of radioactive material. Where radioactive material is still needed, ORS works with industry, law enforcement, and other government organizations to prevent adversaries from acquiring and using high-activity radioactive material by providing cutting edge technologies and capabilities to partners. Enhancing Global Radiological Security Every day in the United States and around the world, vital industries like oil and gas, healthcare, pharmaceutical, and medical research use radioactive material to save lives, fuel progress, and strengthen competitiveness. However, a single incident of radiological terrorism anywhere in the world would have severe economic consequences, create setbacks for the growing demand for peaceful uses of nuclear technologies, and undercut U.S. companies leading innovation in these critical industries. Office of Science User Facilities One important reason for establishing America’s national laboratory system immediately after World War II was to provide a home for large-scale, costly scientific facilities that universities could not afford. Such facilities were believed to be essential to sustaining America’s effort in science. The construction and operation of large-scale scientific user facilities have been integral to the mission of the DOE Office of Science from the earliest days. Today, we maintain and operate 28 DOE Office of Science user facilities at DOE national laboratories across the country as shared resources for the scientific community, with access determined on a competitive basis using peer review. Tens of thousands of researchers make use of these facilities each year. These facilities—including advanced supercomputers, particle accelerators, large x-ray light sources, neutron scattering sources, specialized facilities for nanoscience and genomics, and others—have become increasingly vital tools of scientific discovery. pages.text: Oficina de Normas de Gestión Laboral | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Oficina de Normas de Gestión Laboral La Oficina de Normas de Gestión Laboral (Office of Labor-Management Standards, u OLMS, por sus siglas en inglés) pertenece al Departamento de Trabajo de los Estados Unidos y es responsable de administrar y aplicar la mayoría de las disposiciones de la Ley de Notificación y Divulgación Gestión Laboral (Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act, o LMRDA, por sus siglas en inglés). Dicha ley fue adoptada con el fin de garantizar normas básicas de democracia y responsabilidad fiscal en las organizaciones laborales del sector privado. Los sindicatos que representan a los empleados del Correo Postal de los Estados Unidos también se hallan sujetos a la LMRDA. Los sindicatos de empleados federales se hallan sujetos a normas similares conforme a la Ley de Reforma del Servicio Civil de 1978 (Civil Service Reform Act, o CSRA, por sus siglas in inglés) y a la Ley del Servicio Exterior de 1980. pages.title: Oldest footprints in Saudi Arabia reveal intriguing step in early human migration | National Geographic
pages.description: Animal and human tracks show the lush landscape that may have greeted Homo sapiens as they ventured into new lands more than 100,000 years ago.
pages.text: Oldest footprints in Saudi Arabia reveal intriguing step in early human migration | National Geographic Of the hundreds of fossil footprints found at the Alathar ancient lake deposit in Saudi Arabia, scientists identified seven that were likely made by members of our own species, Homo sapiens. Photograph by Klint Janulis SCIENCE NEWS Oldest footprints in Saudi Arabia reveal intriguing step in early human migration Animal and human tracks show the lush landscape that may have greeted Homo sapiens as they ventured into new lands more than 100,000 years ago. By Maya Wei-Haas Published September 17, 2020 • 9 min read Small oval depressions—376 in all—are scattered across a patch of dry ground nestled between the dunes of northern Saudi Arabia. At a glance, these pockmarks don't seem particularly impressive, so much so that a team of scientists surveying the region almost passed them by in 2017. But upon further examination, the team realized that the depressions were left by an array of ancient animals, and among them were traces of our own species, Homo sapiens . The discovery of human footprints, if confirmed, would mark the oldest trace of our species yet found in the Arabian Peninsula, which sits at the gateway to early humans’ spread around the world. As described in a new study published in Science Advances , the frozen footfalls preserve a striking snapshot of time some 115,000 years ago, as animals and humans congregated near a shallow lake, perhaps with a shared purpose of slaking thirst and sating hunger. Depuis, je consacre mon temps à marcher (sans prétentions de difficultés : pas de montagne, mais quand même de l’ordre de 2000 km par an) et à faire des maths (c’est un passe-temps depuis toujours, principalement en algèbre autour des équations fonctionnelles). J’ai découvert OSM très récemment (printemps 2025) à l’occasion de mon passage de Windows à Linux MINT et de mes premiers essais de smartphone avec un LineageOS (Android déGafamisé). ce qui suit n’engage bien sûr que moi J’ai d’abord considéré qu’il s’agissait d’une application de cartes éditables librement avant de découvrir qu’il s’agit en fait : d’une base de données cartographique mondiale, avec contributions libres, et surtout ne répertoriant et n’exposant que des données libres de droit, sous licences le plus libre possible. d’un considérable écosystème applicatif open-source exploitant cette base de données cartographique pour des utilisations très diverses pour contribuer ou exploiter de façon intelligente et efficace, voire ludique. Pour ceux que j’ai regardés et utilisés : Id, JOSM, OsmTracker, Osmose, StreetComplete, taginfo, overpass, panoramax, NSI Pour ceux que je n’ai fait que survoler pour l’instant : MapRoulette, Mon Commerce OS

Et me voilà parti avec mon smartphone à la main pour photographier chaque point d’apport (en fait une photo par conteneur et une photo pour le point d’apport constitué par le groupe de conteneurs).
